transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-25 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~62 minutes | Recorded on Fireflies
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Arman Patel (Redwood PSM); Priya Nair (CISO, Cascade), Tom Alvarez (Head of Platform), Leah Brooks (Compliance), Omar Reid (SRE Lead), Nina Soto (Procurement)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, optional): Quick security & compliance review focused on incident notification, BCDR/RTO & RPO targets, KMS/customer-managed keys, RBAC/SSO mapping, and audit log retention. Action items agreed to share artifacts and schedule tabletop.

Topics: SOC 2/ISO evidence, RBAC/SSO (SAML/SAML2) mapping, audit logs & log retention, encryption at rest & KMS (customer-managed keys vs Redwood-managed), incident runbook & escalation paths, BCDR RTO/RPO targets, SLA expectations and notification timing.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining on a rainy Wednesday... um, appreciate the time. Quick roll call, we'll do the runbook and K M S stuff and then cover RTO R P O and escalation.
[00:18] Priya: Hi, Priya here. We are mostly focused on compliance — SOC two, ISO, plus legal needs for incident notification. We also need a clear view of KMS handling and if Redwood supports customer-managed keys.
[00:28] Jordan: Perfect. Maya, you want to kick off with the high level on KMS and how keys are used in both Hosted and Private deployments?
[00:34] Maya: Yeah sure. So in Hosted, by default we use Redwood-managed keys that live in our cloud KMS; data is encrypted at rest and in transit. For enterprise Private or VPC deployments we support customer-managed keys — BYOK — via AWS KMS or an external HSM. There's envelope encryption. I should flag that the config differs if you choose Dedicated vs Private. Dedicated can be configured with CMKs if committed contract is in place.
[01:05] Tom: When you say envelope encryption, does Redwood hold any plaintext? What about key rotation and access logs?
[01:12] Maya: We do not hold plaintext for objects that customers mark as customer-managed — the data plane still writes encrypted blobs. Key rotation is supported; you can rotate keys with a grace period. We log KMS API calls in audit logs. Small caveat, sometimes the transcripts show K V cash as K V cache — it's actually K V cache, but with encryption the cache is opaque.
[01:36] Priya: Audit logs — what's retained by default and can we push them to our SIEM? We need at least seven years for certain records per our regulator.
[01:45] Jordan: Defaults are 90 days in the Console UI but we offer log export to S3 or a syslog for archiving. Long-term retention (7+ years) is handled via the export path to your account; we support delivery to your S3 with lifecycle policies.
[02:00] Leah: And are audit logs cryptographically signed or tamper-evident?
[02:05] Maya: We sign logs at ingestion with an integrity hash; there's a chain-of-trust mechanism. When logs are sent to your S3, you can verify the signature. There are occasional misspellings in the system metadata — Fireflies sometimes transcribed "signing" as "sine-ing" in older outputs — but the underlying mechanism is content hash + KMS-wrapped signing.
[02:23] Omar: For incident notification — what are the triggers for Redwood to notify customers? Is it P1 only or P1/P2? How about planned maintenance?
[02:32] Jordan: Our standard is P1/P1A get immediate notification — within the SLA window — and P2 gets notified under certain conditions. We agreed in contract to send notifications via e-mail and pager/SMS for Sev1. For Private deployments you can configure webhook callbacks to your incident system.
[02:47] Priya: We need legal notification windows for breaches — 72 hours to legal + compliance team. Does Redwood have a template notification package?
[02:55] Jordan: Yes, we maintain a breach notification template that we can tailor. It includes affected assets, timeline, root cause (if available), mitigations, and recommended next steps. We'll share the template.
[03:04] Tom: On RTO and RPO — Cascade's baseline requirement for policy is RTO <= 4 hours for critical inference endpoints and RPO <= 1 hour. Can Redwood meet that on Hosted? Dedicated? Private?
[03:16] Maya: On Hosted, typical SLA-backed recovery time for region-level outages is guided by failover policies; for hard failures we have automated region failover to a secondary region and fallback strategies. Realistically, RTO of under 4 hours is achievable with multi-region routing and warm standby for the models you pin. RPO depends on cache and state — for stateless inference it's near-zero; for sessions with KV cache there's up to one hour depending on prefix cache flush and replication config.
[03:46] Priya: So the KV cache replication — is it replicated across regions? We can't lose session state for claims workflows.
[03:53] Maya: KV cache can be replicated to a configured secondary, but you should plan for periodic checkpointing to durable storage. We also have automatic prefix caching which helps but it's not a substitute for real durable session storage.
[04:05] Omar: For on-prem / private deployments, what's the expected RTO for total service restore if a primary cluster has a full hardware failure?
[04:11] Maya: If you're running Private with your own infra, the RTO is a function of your provisioning. Our Private package includes documented playbooks for cold failover; typical target is 4–8 hours for full restore depending on inventory and whether you have warm standby. We recommend Dedicated with cross-zone redundancy for tighter RTOs.
[04:29] Leah: SLA numbers — do you publish an uptime % for inference endpoints? We need that for vendor scoring.
[04:34] Jordan: Our commercial SLA is 99.95% for Dedicated customers on selected plans. Hosted has tiers; public-tier customers see 99.9% SLOs but enterprise contracts can get 99.95% with credits. We can include detailed SLO language in the artifacts.
[04:48] Priya: Escalation chain — show us who Redwood calls, and do we have the ability to pre-seed our legal and ops contact lists into the notification flow?
[04:58] Arman: Yes, you can pre-seed contacts; we support multiple notification channels and an escalation matrix with timeouts. Our standard is immediate notify to the primary contact, then escalations at 15 and 45 minutes for Sev1; for Sev2 we escalate at 60 and 180 minutes. These intervals are configurable in the dedicated contract.
[05:18] Nina: Any SLA credits tied to missed notifications? If Redwood misses a required 72-hour legal notice, what's the recourse?
[05:25] Jordan: That's contract-level. We have contractual clauses for notification obligations; if an operator error prevents notification within agreed windows, we treat that seriously and escalate — remedies may include credits and a post-incident review. Legal wants to review the exact wording; we will share the proposed clause.
[05:38] Priya: Let's talk about RBAC and SSO mapping — we use Okta, and we need SCIM for user provisioning and SAML2 for SSO. Also fine-grained RBAC so only certain teams can kick off model rollouts or change KMS keys.
[05:52] Maya: We support Okta SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning. RBAC is role-based with a least-privilege model — roles like Viewer, Developer, Ops, Admin. We can also map custom roles and bind them to SAML groups. Changing KMS keys requires Admin role plus a 2-person approval workflow for customer-managed key rotation in Private deployments.
[06:12] Tom: Is there an audit trail for who rotated keys and who approved it?
[06:16] Maya: Yep, every action is logged with a user principal and timestamp. For key rotation we write an immutable audit record that includes the key IDs, rotation time, and approver. These are surfaced in the Console as well as exported logs.
[06:27] Priya: How about pen test remediation — do you share your remediation timeline and fixes? We need to see that you close high/critical vuln within X days.
[06:34] Jordan: We share a redacted pen test summary and overall remediation SLA. Historically our high and critical items are triaged with fixes or mitigations within 30 days, with some exceptions based on impact. We'll send the most recent report with redactions.
[06:46] Omar: For tabletop drills, what does Redwood need from us? Our preferred outcome is to validate that legal notification happens within 72 hours and that engineering can failover to the secondary region without data loss.
[06:58] Arman: For tabletop we run through scenarios — P1 region outage, security breach, KMS compromise — and we exercise notification templates, oncall routing, and runbook steps. We'll need your escalation tree, list of SMEs, and a contact to play the role of legal. Good goal to validate both notification and technical failover within your RTO/RPO.
[07:13] Priya: KMS compromise scenario — if a CMK is suspected compromised, do you have a key revocation or rapid rotation path? What's the dependency on cloud provider KMS?
[07:22] Maya: In CMK cases you can schedule a rewrap/rotation. If you use your own AWS CMK, you can disable the key from your account which prevents new decrypt operations, but any existing data encrypted with old key might be impacted. We recommend a dual-wrapping approach where data is encrypted first with a data key and then the data key is KMS-wrapped; rotating the outer wrap is less disruptive. Rapid rotation is possible but must be coordinated — we can provide a runbook.
[07:45] Leah: Legal asks if you will provide a signed attestation for key handling?
[07:49] Jordan: We can provide SOC 2 artifacts and an attestation letter to that effect; for specific KMS key-handling attestations we can negotiate contract language.
[07:58] Priya: Are incident post-mortems shared with customers? What's redaction policy?
[08:03] Arman: Yes, we share post-incident reports with impacted customers. We redact sensitive internal info, but include timeline, root cause, mitigations, and remediation plan. We also share the action-owner tracker.
[08:12] Omar: How are runbooks versioned? We want to make sure that when you update the incident runbook it doesn't silently change behavior for us.
[08:20] Maya: Runbooks are stored in a versioned docs repo. For customers we provide a copy of the runbook pinned at the contract start, and we notify customers of major changes. For critical change we run a change advisory and coordinate a review.
[08:33] Priya: OK can we walk through a mock Sev1 step-by-step — start from detection to customer notification to mitigation?
[08:38] Jordan: Sure. Detection: automated monitors or SRE alerts. Triage: SRE determines Sev1 within 5 minutes and opens an incident ticket. Notification: primary oncall is paged immediately; Redwood also triggers customer webhook and email. Escalation: if not acknowledged in 15 minutes we escalate to oncall lead, and 45 minutes later to engineering director. Simultaneously we run failover playbook or rollback to previous model version. Post-incident: we produce a report within 72 hours and follow-up remediation plan.
[09:08] Tom: That 5-minute triage — is that our SLA or an internal target?
[09:11] Jordan: Internal target; contractually we commit to the notification windows and time-to-ack values are part of operational metrics. We can profile current median times and share them.
[09:20] Priya: Are there any historical incidents of KMS compromise at Redwood?
[09:24] Arman: No compromises of customer CMKs to our knowledge. We had a minor operational miskeying event last year which was caught and rotated. We'll include the redacted post-incident report.
[09:33] Leah: For compliance reviews, do you offer on-site audits or remote access to evidence?
[09:38] Jordan: Remote access to evidence via our compliance portal is standard. On-site audits can be arranged for enterprise clients under NDA.
[09:45] Omar: On the practical side, for our engineers will you provide a dry-run playbook and run a sandbox failover?
[09:51] Maya: Yes — sandbox failovers are part of our onboarding for Dedicated/Private customers. We'll run a simulated failover and share logs.
[09:58] Priya: One more on legal — notification of regulators: do you co-ordinate or just supply data? Sometimes we need the vendor to be directly involved.
[10:06] Jordan: We can coordinate; we typically act as a supporting vendor and provide required artifacts, but we can also participate in regulator conversations if the contract specifies it.
[10:15] Nina: Procurement question — is there a product add-on for extended audit log retention and higher SLA?
[10:19] Jordan: Yes, extended retention, extended SLA tiers, and concierge incident support are add-ons. We'll price those in the follow-up.
[10:26] Priya: Anything else on data residency? Our policy requires EU customer data to remain in EU regions.
[10:31] Maya: We support regional routing and residency. For Hosted we can pin model serving to EU regions; for Private deployments you're already in your VPC so data residency is controlled by you.
[10:40] Tom: For encryption in transit, do you use mTLS for customer-private pipelines?
[10:44] Maya: mTLS is supported for Private and Dedicated inter-service comms and for webhooks if you configure it. Hosted uses TLS 1.2/1.3 with strong ciphers.
[10:52] Priya: Can audit logs be forwarded to our Splunk and do you support structured log schemas?
[10:56] Maya: Yes, we support forwarding and can map to a structured schema; we've done Splunk and Elastic stacks for other clients. We'll include a sample mapping.
[11:05] Jordan: Alright, let's recap and get to the final minute items. Action items: share SOC 2, pen test redacted, runbook docs, KMS guide, schedule tabletop. Any blockers?
[11:15] Priya: No blockers — just need the artifacts and to confirm RTO/RPO for specific endpoints after you share the runbook.
[11:22] Leah: I'll confirm retention numbers internally and get back to you.
[11:26] Omar: I'll send the oncall tree and contacts.
[11:29] Jordan: Great. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the tabletop and send the artifacts. Thanks everyone.
[11:35] Priya: Thanks, bye.

Meeting end.

Post-call notes: transcription has medium quality — several acronyms transcribed imperfectly (SAML -> samble/samble, KMS -> K M S, KV cache -> K V cash). The audio included crosstalk around 07:00–08:00 when legal and SRE were chiming in.
